opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and I think there are a few things that come together.

The first is just stability. A quadruped is fundamentally a much more stable platform. You have four contact points, the center of mass is low, and even if the policy does something slightly off, the robot can usually catch itself. With a humanoid you're balancing on one or two feet, with a high center of mass and a small support polygon. So the margin for error is much smaller, and small mistakes in the reward or in the dynamics quickly turn into falls.

The second is the gap between "it walks" and "it walks well." With quadrupeds, if you train with reinforcement learning and a fairly simple set of rewards, track a velocity command, don't use too much torque, keep the body roughly level, you often get gaits that look pretty natural and work on hardware. With humanoids, RL is very good at finding strange solutions that technically satisfy the objective. You get shuffling, stomping, weird arm motions, leaning, knees locked in odd configurations. So you end up adding a lot more reward terms or motion priors to shape the behavior into something that looks human-like and is also safe for the hardware, and every one of those terms is another knob that interacts with the others.

Third, the hardware itself. Humanoids have more degrees of freedom, more complex mechanisms like parallel linkages in the ankles or knees, and often actuators that are closer to their limits because you're trying to keep the legs light. That makes the sim-to-real gap harder to close. Things like actuator dynamics, joint friction, backlash, foot contact modeling, all matter more when you're dynamically balancing.

And finally, the hardware is just less mature and less forgiving. Quadrupeds have gone through several generations, they're robust, you can let them fall a hundred times. Humanoid falls are more expensive and more dangerous, so iterating on real hardware is slower, and that feedback loop is a big part of tuning.

So it's less that one thing is dramatically harder, and more that every part of the pipeline, the rewards, the simulation fidelity, the hardware, has less slack, and they compound.

r001.rationale: The response cites stability, reward shaping, hardware complexity, and slower iteration as the sources of difficulty. It mentions human-like walking as a reward-shaping concern, but does not identify human expectations as the primary cause.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think there are a few things going on. The first one is just stability. A quadruped is a very forgiving platform. If you give it a terrible policy, it will probably still stand up, it will probably still move forward in some awkward way, and you can iterate from there. A humanoid is inherently unstable. The center of mass is high, the support polygon is small, and the moment the policy makes a mistake the robot is on the floor. So the feedback you get during tuning is much more binary. Either it works or it falls, and that makes it hard to see gradual progress and to understand what to fix.

The second thing is that the gait of a quadruped is, in some sense, easier to discover. If you just reward forward velocity and penalize energy, the learning algorithm will find something that looks like a trot pretty quickly, because that is close to the natural solution for that morphology. For a humanoid, the natural solution that reinforcement learning finds is usually not walking. It will find some shuffling, or hopping, or dragging a foot, because those are easier to learn and they do satisfy the reward. So you end up adding a lot of reward terms to shape the behavior into something that actually looks like a human walking, and every one of those terms is a knob that you have to tune. And they interact with each other, so changing one often breaks another.

And then the third thing is the upper body. On a quadruped the legs are the whole story. On a humanoid you have arms, you have a torso, you have the head, and all of that mass is moving around and affecting the balance. The policy has to coordinate many more degrees of freedom, and you also usually care about what the arms are doing, because you want the robot to be useful and not just flail around. So the problem is higher dimensional, the dynamics are less forgiving, and the target behavior is much more specific. Each of those alone is manageable, but together they make the tuning loop a lot slower and a lot more frustrating than what we were used to with quadrupeds.

r001.rationale: The response mentions shaping a humanoid gait to look like human walking, but presents that as one factor among stability and upper-body complexity. It does not attribute the greater difficulty primarily to humans’ expectations.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest difference is that a humanoid has much less margin for error. With a quadruped, you can keep three feet on the ground and have a fairly stable support region. With a humanoid, when you walk, you spend a lot of time balancing on one foot. So you have to coordinate the motion of the whole body while making sure the next foot lands in the right place.

That makes the tuning more sensitive. You want the robot to track a velocity command, but you also want it to move smoothly, avoid excessive forces, and recover from disturbances. Those objectives interact. If you penalize motion too much, for example, you might prevent it from taking the step it needs to stay upright. And because a humanoid tends to have a higher center of mass, a small mistake can become a fall pretty quickly.

r001.rationale: The response attributes the difficulty to balance demands, interacting control objectives, and a high center of mass. It does not cite people’s expectations for how humanoid robots should walk.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main difference is that a quadruped has a much larger support polygon. You have four feet, and you can often keep three of them on the ground while moving the fourth. So there’s quite a bit of room for error. With a humanoid, you’re spending a lot of time balancing on one foot, and your center of mass is relatively high. A small error can quickly turn into a fall.

That also makes tuning harder because everything is coupled. You want the robot to move forward, but it also has to shift its weight correctly, clear the ground with the swinging foot, and make the next contact at the right time. If you change a reward to improve one of those things, you can make another one worse. And if the robot falls immediately, it doesn’t get much opportunity to discover a better way of walking.

r001.rationale: The response attributes the difficulty to balance, a smaller support polygon, coupled movements, and falls. It does not attribute it to expectations about how humanoid robots should walk.
